title: HPC Workload Characterisation Questionnaire
description: This questionnaire collects factual information about your group's computing workloads. It helps the HPC Users' Committee assess how well the present clusters (Gargi and Raman) meet current needs, and plan for growth. You describe what you observe; the committee applies the agreed tests.
coreNotice: Users provide facts and evidence. The committee applies the agreed tests. You are not being asked to assess your own priority, entitlement, or queue. Incomplete technical knowledge does not disadvantage your submission — 'Don't know' is always a valid answer.

sections.title: B. Your HPC Experience
sections.description:
Please answer from your group's experience on any HPC system you have used — not only the IISER Bhopal clusters (Gargi and Raman). Many groups will be using these clusters for the first time; experience on earlier IISER clusters, national facilities, collaborators' clusters or cloud resources is equally relevant.

Your answers here and in Section C decide which short follow-up sections appear. There is no disadvantage to reporting operational difficulties.

sections.title: C. Your Workloads

Describe up to five main codes your group runs, one entry each. Numbers for a typical job are enough; ticking "Don't know" is always fine.

The committee calculates totals (such as core-hours per year) from these numbers — you do not need to.

Later sections ask about specific codes by picking them from this list.

sections.title: E5. Scratch Storage
sections.description:
Shown because a scratch problem was reported or a workload writes large files while it runs. Scratch is shared, dynamic space; there is a largest area any single user may occupy rather than equal shares. Read-only inputs can usually stay in the home area, which is on the same parallel file system; scratch matters most for files written, or written and re-read, during a run.

Add one entry per workload concerned; only the workloads this applies to.

questions.label: Would assistance with benchmarking any of your codes be useful?
questions.helpText: A benchmark is a representative calculation run on known hardware to measure performance objectively. It is particularly useful if you do not have runtime data from the current cluster. Your answer helps the committee gauge interest; it is not a commitment of support. Any assistance would be arranged separately — for example, with help from experienced users who volunteer.
